summary: This standards-track document describes how data center networks can benefit from non-RBridge nodes doing TRILL encapsulation with help from a directory service. The directory tells those nodes where to send traffic.

eli5.summary: A new delivery helper can look up addresses in a directory instead of learning every street, then wrap packages properly.

questions: how can non-rbridge nodes encapsulate trill
what is a trill encapsulating node
why would a non rbridge encapsulate trill
what is the trill en source nickname
subtitle: How ordinary servers and virtual switches can wrap frames in TRILL headers themselves, using a directory to look up where to send them.

tldr.problem: Making every virtual switch in a huge data center an RBridge could exhaust TRILL nicknames and strain IS-IS, while putting the TRILL edge higher up forces edge RBridges to keep very large MAC and VLAN tables.
tldr.mechanism: A non-RBridge node, called a TRILL-EN, asks a directory which edge RBridge a destination sits behind and then adds the TRILL header itself. It does not take part in IS-IS routing.
tldr.outcome: The TRILL domain can stay a reasonable size and switches on bridged LANs need fewer MAC entries. The RFC warns that TRILL-ENs can forge headers, so they should be trusted nodes.

today: RFC 8380 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2018. The metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 8380 describes how data center networks can benefit from non-RBridge nodes doing TRILL encapsulation with help from a directory service, and it specifies a method for them to do so.

RFC 7067 and RFC 8171 describe the framework and methods for edge RBridges to get a (MAC and VLAN) to edge RBridge mapping from a directory instead of flooding frames with unknown destination MAC addresses across a TRILL domain. The RFC's observation is that if a node has the needed directory information, any node, even one that is not an RBridge, can perform the TRILL data packet encapsulation.
sections.eli5: If you have a phone book that tells you where everyone lives, you do not need to be a postal worker to address a parcel correctly.

sections.title: Terms Used
sections.content:
The central new term is the TRILL-EN (TRILL Encapsulating Node): a node that performs TRILL encapsulation but does not participate in an RBridge's IS-IS routing. Other terms the RFC defines are AF (the Appointed Forwarder RBridge port), Bridge (a device compliant with IEEE 802.1Q, used interchangeably with Layer 2 switch) and Host (a physical server or a virtual machine running applications).

The RFC uses the RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 key words (MUST, SHOULD and so on) only when they appear in capitals.
sections.eli5: A TRILL-EN is a helper who knows how to put the special shipping label on a parcel but is not part of the delivery company's planning meetings.

sections.title: Directory Assistance for Non-RBridge Nodes
sections.content:
With directory assistance, a non-RBridge node can learn whether a data packet needs to cross the RBridge domain and, if so, which egress RBridge to use. In the example data center, the RBridge domain boundary starts at the network switches rather than at the virtual switches embedded on servers. The directory supplies the nickname of the egress RBridge edge where the destination is attached. The remaining information is learned either by listening to TRILL ES-IS and/or IS-IS Hellos, which show the MAC address and nickname of the local edge RBridges, or by configuration.

A TRILL-EN can pull the mapping from directory servers, and to do so it MUST support TRILL ES-IS. When it receives or generates a native Ethernet frame, it checks its mapping and encapsulates if an entry is found. If the destination MAC and VLAN are not in the table and no pull request gets a positive reply, the frame is either dropped or forwarded in native form to an edge RBridge, depending on configuration.

If the directory does not say whether a destination is behind an edge RBridge, the node can send the frame natively without a TRILL header, or discard it if the directory is known to be complete.

On the RBridge side, a pre-encapsulated packet arriving at the ingress RBridge gets the usual TRILL processing and is forwarded toward the egress nickname in the header. The RFC points to item 8 of Section 4.6.2 of RFC 6325, which lets an RBridge port be configured to accept TRILL-encapsulated frames from a neighbor that is not an RBridge. At the egress, processing is exactly as normal: the RBridge decapsulates the frame and forwards it. If the inner destination MAC is not in its local tables, it floods the frame in the VLAN or drops it, depending on policy.

Nodes can connect to several edge RBridges, through multiple ports or a bridged LAN, and all edge ports on one bridged LAN can receive and forward pre-encapsulated traffic. AF ports are still needed so that multi-destination packets leave the TRILL campus through only one RBridge.
sections.eli5: The helper looks the street up in the directory, puts the right label on the parcel, and drops it with the nearest sorting centre. If the directory has no answer, the helper either throws the parcel away or hands it over unlabeled, whichever the rules say.

sections.title: Choosing the Source Nickname
sections.content:
A TRILL header holds an ingress (source) nickname and an egress (destination) nickname. A TRILL-EN does not have a nickname of its own. When it adds a TRILL header, it sets the ingress nickname to a nickname of the AF for the data packet's VLAN.

It finds the AF by snooping on IS-IS Hellos from the edge RBridges on its link, in the same way the RBridges determine the AF under RFC 8139. The TRILL-EN is free to send the encapsulated frame to any of the edge RBridges on its link.
sections.eli5: The helper has no return address of its own, so it writes the address of the sorting centre it works with on the parcel.

sections.title: Why Let Non-RBridges Encapsulate
sections.content:
Avoiding nickname exhaustion. For a large data center with hundreds of thousands of virtualized servers, making the virtual switches RBridges would create a TRILL domain with hundreds of thousands of RBridge nodes, which could lead to nickname exhaustion and challenges for IS-IS. Moving the TRILL boundary up to aggregation switches avoids that but forces edge RBridges to maintain very large mapping tables. With pre-encapsulation, all the TRILL-ENs attached to one RBridge can be represented by one TRILL nickname.

Smaller MAC tables on bridged LANs. The RFC gives a worked example: an Access Switch with 40 physical servers, each with 100 VMs, has 4000 hosts. In the worst case all belong to different VLANs, and with 200 hosts per VLAN the switch's MAC table could hold 200 * 4000 = 800,000 entries. When virtual switches pre-encapsulate, the outer destination MAC is that of the local edge RBridge, so local switches do not need entries for remote hosts.

The RFC also notes that decapsulated traffic arriving from other RBridges carries true source and destination MACs, so local bridges can still learn remote hosts. Two remedies are mentioned: disable data-plane learning on local bridges and pre-configure local host MACs with directory help, or have the server use its own MAC as the source address for traffic from its VMs, with the egress node using the destination IP and the directory to build the final Ethernet header.
sections.eli5: If every parcel for far-away places goes in a big labeled box addressed to your local depot, the neighborhood post offices do not each need to memorize every faraway house.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
Directory assistance is required for a non-TRILL node to pre-encapsulate packets for remote RBridges, and TRILL-ENs have the same configuration options as any pull directory client (see Section 4 of RFC 8171).

The security risks all come from the TRILL-EN being able to write the headers. An untrusted TRILL-EN can forge ingress and egress nicknames. With data-plane learning, a forged ingress nickname makes the egress RBridge learn the wrong place for the inner source MAC, so later traffic goes to the wrong RBridge. For that reason an RBridge port should not accept encapsulated frames on a link without an RBridge adjacency unless the end stations on that link are trusted. TRILL-ENs can also forge inner MAC addresses and send in any VLAN, so they must be trusted to enforce VLAN-based policy.

The RFC says spoofing cannot cause persistently looping traffic, because the TRILL header has a hop count, and multi-destination packets are further protected by a Reverse Path Forwarding Check. A TRILL-EN also learns edge RBridge MAC addresses and egress nicknames, which reveals a good deal about the domain's topology. If the path to the directory is attacked, false mappings could be sent, so a combination of authentication and encryption is RECOMMENDED between the directory and the TRILL-EN, and end-to-end encryption and authentication should be considered. This document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: A helper who can write any label can also write a wrong one, so you should only let helpers you trust do it, and make sure the phone book itself cannot be tampered with.
